research.notes: 2026 depth synthesis (web-verified 2026-06-14) for moving value, tokens, NFTs, and contract calls between XRPL mainnet and the XRPL EVM sidechain. HEADLINE STATE: the XRPL EVM Sidechain went LIVE on mainnet 2025-06-30 (Peersyst build on evmOS / Cosmos SDK + CometBFT, PoA validator set, ~3.5s blocks, sub-4s finality, ~1000 TPS, XRP as the native gas token). The bridge to XRPL mainnet is Axelar, integrated via Axelar's NEW Amplifier path (verifier-set + Amplifier Gateway) rather than the legacy validator-coordination flow — XRPL EVM was one of the first Amplifier integrations alongside Stellar Soroban and Movement chains. Two distinct primitives ride that bridge and must not be conflated: (1) the Interchain Token Service (ITS) for moving fungible value — native XRP, XRPL IOUs, and ERC-20s; and (2) General Message Passing (GMP) for arbitrary cross-chain contract calls and token+message combos (callContractWithToken). MECHANICS THAT MATTER TO A STUDIO: bridging XRP from XRPL→EVM is a single Payment to the Axelar Multisig account on XRPL with hex-encoded Memos (call type, destination chain 'xrpl-evm', recipient EVM address, gas); the relayer approves it at the EVM-side Amplifier Gateway and ITS credits the recipient. Reverse (EVM→XRPL) is an interchainTransfer() call naming destinationChain 'xrpl' and an r-address. Real-world cost & latency via Squid (the official Axelar-powered UI): typically < 1 XRP and ~3 minutes end-to-end; the underlying XRPL legs are sub-cent / 3-5s but the cross-chain confirmation dominates. KEY NUANCE ON 'WRAPPED': XRP on the EVM side is NOT a wrapped ERC-20 you hold — it is the native gas/value token (sometimes called eXRP in marketing). Bridged XRPL IOUs and inbound ERC-20s DO appear as ERC-20 token contracts registered through ITS. TRUST MODEL (the load-bearing part): Axelar is a Tendermint PoS L1 (~70 validators mid-2026) using quadratic voting (vote weight = sqrt(stake)) and weighted-threshold multisig to co-authorize every cross-chain message — this is an external-committee trust assumption layered on top of XRPL's own consensus, NOT a native XRPL guarantee. The single biggest practical risk for game builders is RECEIVER-SIDE: the Feb-2026 CrossCurve exploit ($3M) drained funds because a custom AxelarExecutable receiver exposed a public execute path WITHOUT validating that the message actually came from the Gateway and from a trusted source chain/address — Axelar core was not breached. Any game contract that mints assets or moves value on _execute / _executeWithToken MUST verify sourceChain + sourceAddress against an allowlist. CROSS-CHAIN GAME PATTERN: keep canonical NFT ownership as native XLS-20 NFTs on XRPL mainnet (cheap, auction-native, no gas-token exposure) and run mutable game logic in Solidity on the EVM side, using GMP to relay 'player X owns asset Y, do Z' rather than physically bridging the NFT every interaction — bridging the asset itself is a lock/mint round-trip with full bridge latency and trust exposure on every move. Wormhole and native IBC are additional/alternative transports the sidechain also supports, but Axelar is the canonical, Ripple-blessed bridge for XRPL↔EVM value.

capabilities.summary: The set of Axelar smart contracts on the XRPL EVM Sidechain that govern fungible-value movement: native XRP, XRPL IOUs (issued currencies), and inbound ERC-20s. XRPL→EVM is a single Payment to the Axelar Multisig account on XRPL carrying hex Memos (call type, destinationChain 'xrpl-evm', recipient EVM address, gas); the relayer approves at the Amplifier Gateway and ITS credits the destination. THE REPRESENTATION RULE a studio must internalize: native XRP arrives on the EVM side as the NATIVE gas/value token (not a wrapped ERC-20 balance you manage); by contrast a bridged XRPL IOU or an inbound ERC-20 is represented as an ERC-20 token contract registered through ITS with an Axelar tokenId. capabilities.name: General Message Passing (GMP) — cross-chain contract calls
capabilities.summary: The primitive for sending ARBITRARY data and function calls across chains — the heart of any 'native XRPL ownership + EVM game logic' design. From XRPL, you submit a Payment (min 1 drop if no asset moves) to the Axelar Multisig account with Memos carrying the call type, destination chain, target contract address, and an ABI-encoded payload hash (encode with ethers AbiCoder). Axelar verifies and relays; the EVM-side Amplifier Gateway records ContractCallApproved; the relayer triggers execute() on your AxelarExecutable contract, passing commandId, sourceChain ('xrpl'), sourceAddress (the originating r-account), and the ABI payload. This lets an XRPL-side event ('player listed asset', 'player paid entry') drive Solidity game logic without bridging the asset itself — the recommended low-trust pattern. Confirmation is typically a few minutes (bridge-dominated, not block-time-dominated).

key_fields.reach: 70+ chains as of 2026 (Ethereum, rollups, Solana, Sui, Aptos, Stellar, Cosmos/IBC)

capabilities.gotchas: RECEIVER-SIDE VALIDATION IS THE WHOLE GAME. The Feb-2026 CrossCurve exploit ($3M) happened because a custom receiver exposed a callable execute path that did NOT verify the message came from the Gateway nor check sourceChain/sourceAddress — anyone could forge a payload. Axelar core was not breached; the bug was integration-side. EVERY game contract that mints assets, grants entitlements, or moves value in execute()/_executeWithToken() MUST (a) be invoked only via the Gateway and (b) allowlist sourceChain == 'xrpl' AND sourceAddress == your known XRPL account. Also: GMP is asynchronous and can get stuck mid-flight — never design logic that assumes synchronous round-trips or instant confirmation.

capabilities.name: callContractWithToken — value + message in one hop
capabilities.summary: The GMP variant that delivers a fungible token transfer AND an arbitrary payload to the destination contract in a single cross-chain message. The receiver inherits AxelarExecutableWithToken and implements _executeWithToken(commandId, sourceChain, sourceAddress, payload, tokenSymbol, amount), which fires with both the credited tokens and your custom bytes. For games this collapses two-step flows into one atomic-feeling hop: 'send 10 XRP entry fee AND register the player into match #42', 'deposit soft-currency AND mint the crafted item'. It removes the race window where value has arrived but the triggering call hasn't (or vice versa), which otherwise forces awkward reconciliation. Useful but a notch below raw GMP and ITS because many game designs deliberately keep value on XRPL and pass only messages — paying gas + bridge fees to move tokens every interaction is often the wrong economy.

key_fields.use: value transfer bundled with an instruction (entry fee + action, deposit + mint)
key_fields.atomicity: tokens and payload delivered together — removes value/instruction race window

capabilities.gotchas: Same receiver-side validation rule as raw GMP, but the stakes are higher because tokens are physically present — a missing sourceChain/sourceAddress allowlist check here means an attacker can both forge the instruction AND have your contract treat fabricated tokens as real. Validate the tokenSymbol/amount against expectations, not just the payload. Bundling value into every call means every interaction pays bridge + gas fees and incurs ~minutes latency — only use it when value genuinely must cross; otherwise prefer message-only GMP with assets parked on XRPL.

capabilities.name: Native XLS-20 ownership + EVM game logic (cross-chain pattern)
capabilities.summary: The recommended architecture for a cross-chain game: keep CANONICAL asset ownership as native XLS-20 NFTs on XRPL mainnet (cheap mint, built-in on-ledger offers/auctions, transfer fees, no gas-token exposure, mature secondary-market tooling) and run MUTABLE game logic — combat resolution, durability, leveling, marketplaces, matchmaking — in Solidity on the EVM sidechain. Instead of physically bridging the NFT on every interaction (a lock/mint round-trip with full bridge latency and trust exposure each time), use GMP to relay attestations: 'r-address X owns XLS-20 NFT Y, grant entitlement Z'. The NFT never leaves XRPL; the EVM contract reacts to verified ownership messages. This minimizes the value sitting under bridge trust at any moment, keeps the scarce/tradeable layer on the chain best suited for it, and isolates the EVM side to logic + ephemeral state. It is the concrete answer to 'native XRPL NFT ownership + EVM-contract game logic'.

capabilities.gotchas: Ownership attestation is a SNAPSHOT — by the time the GMP message lands (~minutes), the player could have sold/transferred the XLS-20 NFT on XRPL. For entitlements where staleness matters, require a fresh attestation at point-of-use, escrow/lock the NFT on XRPL while the EVM entitlement is active, or accept the staleness window explicitly. If you DO mint an ERC-721 mirror on the EVM side, you now have two representations and must prevent double-spend (the canonical NFT must be locked/escrowed on XRPL while the mirror exists). The attesting XRPL account and message path are still subject to all the receiver-side validation rules — a forged 'X owns Y' message is as dangerous as forged value.

capabilities.name: Axelar trust & security model (PoS committee, quadratic voting)
capabilities.status: live (external trust assumption — must be threat-modeled)
capabilities.summary: The actual security guarantee behind every XRPL↔EVM movement, and the part most easily glossed over. Axelar is a Tendermint Proof-of-Stake L1 (~70 active validators mid-2026) whose validators/verifiers run light clients or nodes for connected chains and stake AXL. Every cross-chain message must be co-authorized by a weighted-threshold quorum using QUADRATIC VOTING — each validator's vote weight equals the square root of its stake, which caps the influence of large stakers and pushes toward broader collusion requirements. For XRPL EVM specifically, this runs through the Amplifier verifier set + per-chain Amplifier Gateway. The honest framing for a studio: this is 'an L1's trust model applied to messaging' — strictly weaker than XRPL's own consensus for assets that have crossed, because it adds an external committee you must now also trust to be live and honest. Knowing this bounds how much irreversible value you let ride the bridge and informs your compensator design.

The dominant real-world failure in 2026 was integration-side (receiver contracts trusting unauthenticated messages), not core-protocol breaks — but core risks (governance capture via flash-loaned voting power, verifier collusion, prolonged halts) are non-zero and would affect ALL in-flight value at once. Bridges led 2026 exploit losses ($328M+ by mid-year). Cap bridged value, prefer message-only patterns over moving assets, and build manual reconciliation for stuck transfers.

research.notes: Wave-6 depth synthesis, web-verified mid-2026. The XRPL EVM Sidechain went LIVE on mainnet on 2025-06-30 (chain ID 1440000; testnet 1449000). It is a standalone Cosmos-SDK/EVM L1 with XRP as the native gas token, ~3–5s finality, ~1000 TPS target. EVM is currently at the Paris hard fork with solc ≤ 0.8.24 (a Prague + solc 0.8.30 upgrade is staged) — this is the single most load-bearing constraint for game builders: pin your pragma to ^0.8.24 and verify any OpenZeppelin/library version compiles under Paris (PUSH0/transient-storage opcodes from Cancun are NOT yet guaranteed). Everything ordinary on EVM deploys natively: ERC-20 (game currency), ERC-721 (unique items), ERC-1155 (mixed fungible+NFT inventories — the right default for game item systems because one contract holds stackable consumables AND unique gear with batch mint/transfer). The native-vs-EVM decision is the spine of this lane: XLS-20 NFTs and IOU/MPT tokens live on the XRPL mainnet (cheap, no gas, protocol-level features like authorized-minter, transfer fees, native DEX) and bridge across via Axelar Interchain Token Service (ITS); ERC-721/ERC-20 live on the sidechain (full Solidity composability — crafting, marketplaces, escrow, on-chain logic). CRITICAL bridge limit verified mid-2026: Axelar ITS bridges FUNGIBLE assets only — native XRP, XRPL IOUs, and ERC-20 — there is NO NFT bridge. XLS-20 NFTs do NOT cross to ERC-721 and vice-versa; choose the chain per asset up front. For on-chain randomness (loot, crafting, gacha): there is NO Chainlink VRF on XRPL EVM as of mid-2026. Band Protocol is the integrated oracle (price feeds live; Band also offers Band VRF on other chains but VRF is NOT confirmed deployed on XRPL EVM mainnet) — treat verifiable randomness as a gap requiring a commit-reveal pattern, an off-chain signed-RNG oracle, or porting Pyth Entropy / Band VRF yourself; NEVER use block.timestamp/blockhash for valuable loot. Account abstraction (ERC-4337) is chain-agnostic and needs no protocol change, so gasless/sponsored-gas player UX is deployable today by standing up your own EntryPoint+bundler+paymaster (no first-party AA infra is bundled). Upgradeable contracts: OpenZeppelin 5.x recommends UUPS (cheaper, ERC-7201 namespaced storage) over Transparent — but verify the OZ release you pin compiles under Paris/0.8.24.

capabilities.name: ERC-1155 multi-token contract for mixed game inventories
capabilities.summary: ERC-1155 holds many token IDs in ONE contract where each ID can be fungible (stackable potions, ore, gold-shards), semi-fungible (event tickets), or non-fungible (unique gear, supply=1). This is the correct default for a game item system on the sidechain: a single deploy covers your whole inventory, and batch mint/batch transfer move dozens of item types in one tx — decisive for gas and for atomic loot drops/crafting outputs. Native EVM, deploys today on mainnet (chain 1440000) under solc ≤0.8.24.
gotchas: Pin pragma to ^0.8.24 and use an OpenZeppelin version that compiles under the Paris EVM (no Cancun PUSH0/transient-storage assumptions) — the sidechain is Paris until the staged Prague/0.8.30 upgrade lands.
ERC-1155 has NO per-token name/symbol metadata field like ERC-721; it uses a single uri() with {id} substitution. Plan your metadata service for hex-padded 64-char token IDs.
A receiving CONTRACT must implement onERC1155Received / onERC1155BatchReceived or the safe transfer reverts — marketplaces/escrow you write must implement IERC1155Receiver.
ERC-1155 NFTs do NOT bridge to XLS-20 on XRPL mainnet — Axelar ITS is fungible-only. If an item must live as a native XRPL NFT, mint it there, not here.

capabilities.name: Native-vs-EVM asset decision: XLS-20 NFT vs ERC-721
capabilities.summary: The first architectural fork for every game asset: mint the unique item as an XLS-20 NFT on XRPL mainnet, or as an ERC-721 on the EVM sidechain? XLS-20 wins on cost (no gas; tiny reserve), built-in protocol features (authorized minter, on-ledger transfer-fee royalties, native NFT DEX/brokered sales) and reach (6M+ XRPL wallets) — but it is NOT Turing-complete: you cannot run crafting/upgrade/marketplace LOGIC against it on-ledger. ERC-721 wins on composability (any Solidity contract can read/move it — crafting that burns 3 NFTs to mint 1, escrowed PvP wagers, on-chain auction houses, DeFi collateral) but costs gas and lives behind the bridge. CRITICAL: Axelar ITS is fungible-only — there is NO XLS-20<->ERC-721 bridge mid-2026, so this is a one-time, per-asset commitment, not a 'move it later' choice.
key_fields: XLS-20: NFTokenMint, NFTokenMinter, TransferFee, tfTransferable, NFTokenID
ERC-721: tokenURI, ownerOf, safeTransferFrom, approve, _mint, supportsInterface
decision axes: gas cost, composability, royalty enforcement, wallet reach, bridgeability
gotchas: NO NFT bridge: XLS-20 NFTs cannot be moved to ERC-721 (or back) via Axelar ITS as of mid-2026. Pick the chain per asset before minting; design a 'twin mint' or oracle-attestation pattern if an item needs presence on both.
ERC-721 royalties are a marketplace social convention (EIP-2981 is a hint, not enforced); XLS-20 TransferFee is enforced at the protocol level. If enforced royalties matter, that argues for XLS-20.
ERC-721 on the sidechain costs gas to mint and transfer (paid in XRP); high-volume free drops are cheaper as XLS-20 — or as ERC-1155 if they live on EVM.
On-chain game logic (crafting/marketplace/escrow) can ONLY operate on the EVM-side asset; an XLS-20 item is inert from a Solidity standpoint.

Items that feed Solidity crafting/marketplace logic (choose ERC-721)
High-volume, royalty-enforced, low-cost collectibles (choose XLS-20)

capabilities.name: Native-vs-EVM currency decision: IOU/MPT vs ERC-20
capabilities.summary: Where does your soft/hard game currency live? On XRPL mainnet as an IOU (trustline token) or MPT (multi-purpose token): no gas, native DEX, AMM, clawback/freeze/transfer-fee controls, RLUSD settlement, 6M+ wallets — but inert to Solidity. Or on the sidechain as an ERC-20: full composability with crafting/marketplace/escrow/DeFi contracts, approve+transferFrom flows, staking — but every transfer costs XRP gas. Unlike NFTs, currency CAN move: Axelar ITS bridges native XRP, XRPL IOUs, and ERC-20s, so a token can have an IOU representation on XRPL and an ERC-20 representation on the sidechain, kept in sync by the bridge. The decision is therefore 'primary home + bridged shadow,' and the test is whether the currency needs to be an argument to EVM contract logic (→ ERC-20 primary) or just held/traded/paid (→ IOU/MPT primary).
key_fields: ERC-20: balanceOf, transfer, approve, transferFrom, allowance, decimals, totalSupply
IOU: TrustSet, issuer, currency code, transfer rate, RequireAuth, NoFreeze
MPT (XLS-33): MPTokenIssuanceCreate, MPTokenAuthorize, flags (CanClawback, CanTransfer, CanLock)
gotchas: Decimals mismatch: ERC-20 typically 18 decimals; XRPL IOUs use 15 significant digits and MPTs a fixed scale. The bridge handles scaling but rounding/dust at the boundary must be tested before launch.
Bridged supply is split across two chains — your accounting must treat the ITS-locked balance and the minted shadow as one economy or you will double-count treasury.
ERC-20 has no protocol-level clawback/freeze; if regulatory or anti-cheat clawback matters, the IOU/MPT side is the control point (CanClawback flag), not the ERC-20.
Every ERC-20 transfer burns XRP gas; high-frequency micro-rewards are far cheaper as IOU/MPT payments on XRPL mainnet (settle off-chain, batch in, or keep currency native).

capabilities.name: On-chain game logic in Solidity: crafting, marketplace, escrow
capabilities.summary: The reason to be on the EVM side at all: arbitrary game logic the XRPL base layer can't express. Crafting = burn N input ERC-1155/721 tokens, mint an output (atomic, verifiable recipes). Marketplace/auction house = list, bid, settle ERC-721/1155 against ERC-20 in one contract with on-chain fee splits. Escrow = trustless P2P item-for-currency or item-for-item swaps and PvP wagers held by contract until conditions resolve. All are standard EVM patterns (OpenZeppelin building blocks) and deploy on mainnet today; the contract is the referee, removing the studio as a trusted middleman. Escrow MUST have an expiry/timeout refund path or items can be locked forever if the counterparty griefs — there is no protocol-level escrow expiry like XRPL's native EscrowCreate; you implement it.
Marketplace approvals: a player setApprovalForAll to your marketplace is a standing risk; scope approvals and let players revoke. Audit the listing-cancellation race.
On-chain crafting that consumes randomness (e.g., upgrade success%) inherits the VRF gap — see the randomness capability; never seed it from block data.

capabilities.name: Verifiable randomness for loot/gacha — VRF gap and commit-reveal
capabilities.summary: Honest mid-2026 state: there is NO first-party Chainlink-VRF-style verifiable randomness on XRPL EVM. Band Protocol is the integrated oracle, but only price feeds (XRP/BTC/ETH USD) are confirmed live; Band also publishes Band VRF on other chains and Pyth offers Pyth Entropy, but neither VRF is confirmed deployed/callable on XRPL EVM mainnet. Yet loot drops, gacha, crit rolls, and crafting-success need fairness players can audit. The deployable answers today: (1) commit-reveal — players/server commit a hashed seed, reveal later, combine; (2) an off-chain signed-RNG oracle the contract verifies via ECDSA; (3) self-host/port Pyth Entropy's commit-reveal or a Band VRF consumer if/when a coordinator is live. gotchas: Do NOT assume Chainlink VRF exists here — it does not as of mid-2026. Verify any VRF coordinator address is actually deployed on chain 1440000 before designing around it.
Naive commit-reveal lets the last revealer abort to avoid a bad outcome ('last-revealer' grief). Add a deposit/penalty or a default-on-timeout outcome.
Single signed-RNG oracle is a centralization/trust point — disclose it; a malicious or compromised signer can pick outcomes. Consider multi-sig or threshold signatures.
Pyth Entropy/Band VRF have request fees and a callback latency (not same-block) — design loot UX for async resolution.

capabilities.name: Account abstraction (ERC-4337) for gasless player UX
capabilities.summary: ERC-4337 brings smart-contract wallets + sponsored gas WITHOUT any chain protocol change — it runs on any EVM chain via a singleton EntryPoint, off-chain bundlers, and paymasters. For games this is the onboarding unlock: players never need to acquire XRP for gas, can sign UserOperations with a session key, and the studio's paymaster covers the bill (free-to-play feel). Because it needs no first-party support, you can stand it up on XRPL EVM today — but note there is no bundled AA infra: you (or a third-party AA provider) must run an EntryPoint deployment, a bundler, and a paymaster. Pair with session keys so a player approves a play session once instead of signing every move.
gotchas: No first-party 4337 infra on XRPL EVM: you must deploy/point at an EntryPoint, run a bundler, and operate a paymaster — verify the EntryPoint address you target is actually deployed on chain 1440000.
Paymaster = you pay XRP gas for users; an unguarded paymaster is a drain/DoS vector. Rate-limit, allowlist target contracts, and cap per-user sponsorship.
Session keys reduce signing friction but widen blast radius if leaked — scope them tightly (which contracts, value caps, expiry).
AA wallets are contracts, not EOAs; some tooling/explorers and signature checks (ERC-1271) must be handled accordingly in your backend.

best_for.purpose: Onboarding non-crypto players without making them buy gas (sponsored gas)

capabilities.name: Upgradeable game contracts (UUPS proxy, OpenZeppelin 5.x)
capabilities.summary: Live games patch balance, fix bugs, and add seasons — upgradeable proxies let a deployed game contract change logic while preserving state (player balances, item ownership). OpenZeppelin 5.x recommends UUPS over Transparent: cheaper to deploy (no ProxyAdmin), upgrade authority lives in the implementation, and storage uses ERC-7201 namespaced layout so you add state without collision. Standard pattern, deploys on the sidechain today. The tradeoff: upgradeability is also a trust/centralization surface — players are trusting whoever holds the upgrade key. Gate it behind a timelock + multisig and disclose it, or make critical asset contracts immutable.
gotchas: Verify the OpenZeppelin Upgradeable release you pin compiles under solc 0.8.24 / Paris on XRPL EVM — newer OZ minor versions may assume Cancun opcodes.
Constructors don't run behind a proxy — use initializer functions and _disableInitializers() in the implementation, or the implementation can be hijacked.
Storage-layout mistakes on upgrade silently corrupt player balances/ownership. Use the OZ upgrades plugin's storage-layout check in CI on every upgrade.

An upgradeable item/currency contract means the team can rewrite the rules — for player-trust-critical assets consider immutability, or at minimum a timelock so players can exit before a change takes effect.

capabilities.name: Security & audit considerations for game contracts
capabilities.summary: Game contracts hold real player value (items, currency, marketplace escrow) and are immutable-by-default once deployed — security is not optional. The XRPL-EVM-specific layer on top of standard Solidity hygiene: (1) the Paris/solc-0.8.24 constraint — audit that every dependency compiles for the target EVM, since a contract relying on Cancun opcodes can misbehave; (2) the randomness gap — never seed loot from block data; (3) bridge trust — ITS-bridged value depends on Axelar's validator set; (4) upgrade keys are a governance attack surface. Standard must-haves: ReentrancyGuard + Checks-Effects-Interactions, pull-payment, role-gated mint with a multisig, escrow timeouts, and a third-party audit + testnet (chain 1449000) soak before any contract custodies value.

Compiling for the wrong EVM target (assuming Cancun when the chain is Paris) can produce a contract that reverts or behaves unexpectedly — set evmVersion explicitly in Hardhat/Foundry config.
Unbounded mint/upgrade keys are the highest-severity finding in game contracts (infinite-inflation / rule-rewrite rug). Gate behind multisig + timelock and disclose.
Immutability cuts both ways: a bug in a non-upgradeable item contract is permanent. Decide upgradeability deliberately and document the key holders for player trust.

research.notes: 2026 synthesis. The XRPL EVM sidechain is LIVE on mainnet — it launched 30 June 2025 (announced at Cosmos Sovereign EVM Day during EthCC, Cannes), after a public testnet that opened in March 2025 and processed 10M+ transactions. It is a standalone Layer-1 built on the Cosmos SDK + CometBFT (Tendermint BFT consensus) with the evmOS / Cosmos EVM module supplying full Ethereum equivalence; engineered by Peersyst Technology with RippleX, Axelar, and Common Prefix. Mainnet is EVM chain ID 1440000 (RPC https://rpc.xrplevm.org, Blockscout explorer https://explorer.xrplevm.org); testnet is chain ID 1449000 (https://rpc.testnet.xrplevm.org); a devnet exists at 1440002. XRP is the NATIVE gas token — it is bridged onto the sidechain via Axelar (the XRPL<->sidechain interoperability provider), so paying gas means spending bridged XRP, and the displayed currency symbol is XRP. Solidity tooling is fully standard: as of mid-2026 the supported EVM target is Paris with solc <= 0.8.24, with an announced upgrade (post Cosmos-EVM bump) to the Prague EVM target and solc 0.8.30 — a real, load-bearing gotcha because compiling for shanghai/cancun/prague opcodes before the upgrade lands will fail or deploy broken bytecode. research.notes: Mid-2026 depth synthesis of Xahau Hooks, verified against docs.xahau.network (which 301-redirects to xahau.network/docs), the XRPL Hooks readme mirror (xrpl-hooks.readme.io), and the Xahau GitHub org. Hooks are Layer-1 WebAssembly modules attached to accounts that run inside consensus and can REJECT a transaction before it is applied — this is the load-bearing distinction from EVM/L2 smart contracts and the reason Hooks live on Xahau rather than XRPL mainnet (XRPL declined to amend Hooks into core; Xahau is the rippled fork that did, mainnet-live since Oct 2023). C-to-WASM is the production-blessed path; the worst-case execution cost of every hook must be statically knowable, which forces the _g() loop-guard discipline (no Turing-complete unbounded loops) and drives a deterministic up-front fee. As of mid-2026, JSHooks (QuickJS-based JavaScript hooks) is alpha on a dedicated JSHooks testnet only — NOT on Xahau mainnet, gated on a security audit per the roadmap; do not architect a shipping game economy on JSHooks yet. For a game studio: strong-execution hooks are a genuine on-chain enforcement primitive (block disallowed transfers, gate NFT trades, enforce royalties at the ledger level) but the 10-hook chain, ~256-byte state values, 32-byte keys, capped emission generation (≤10) and 5-ledger emit window are hard design constraints that make hooks a rules/guardrail layer, not a general compute layer.

capabilities.name: Hooks execution model (Layer-1 WASM transaction interceptor)
capabilities.summary: Hooks are small WebAssembly modules installed on a Xahau account that execute as part of consensus whenever a transaction touches that account. Because they run BEFORE the originating transaction is applied (for strong stakeholders), a hook can rollback and completely block a transaction — this Layer-1 'decide if a transaction is allowed in the first place' semantics is the core differentiator from EVM/L2 smart contracts that only react after the fact. The hook entry points are hook(uint32_t reserved) and the callback cbak(uint32_t); a hook terminates with accept() (allow), rollback() (reject + revert), or errors out.
capabilities.gotchas: A hook is NOT general-purpose compute: it cannot make network calls, cannot loop without a guard, and has a statically-bounded worst-case execution. Reverting via rollback() reverts the whole originating transaction for strong stakeholders only; weak-executed hooks run after application and cannot block. Errors (not just rollback) also fail the hook — there is no silent failure.

best_for.purpose: On-ledger enforcement of transfer/trade rules that cannot be bypassed by the client
Gating or taxing in-game economy transfers at the protocol level
Compliance gates (allowlist/blocklist) enforced before settlement

sources.title: Transactional Stakeholders — Strong vs Weak Execution (XRPL Hooks)
sources.claim: Strong execution runs before the transaction applies and can rollback() to block it; weak execution runs after and cannot rollback. The reserved param signals 0=strong, 1=weak, 2=weak-following-strong.

capabilities.name: SetHook transaction (definitions, install/update/delete)
capabilities.summary: SetHook is the transaction that installs, updates, or removes hooks on an account. CreateCode carries hex WASM bytecode for a new hook; identical bytecode is de-duplicated into a shared reference-counted HookDefinition ledger object, and other accounts install by HookHash instead of re-uploading code. SetHook submits an array (the hook chain) and supports four operations — Create, Install (by hash), Update (params/grants/namespace), and Delete (hsfOVERRIDE + empty CreateCode, which decrements the refcount).
capabilities.gotchas: Deleting a hook requires hsfOVERRIDE AND an empty-string CreateCode at that position; just omitting it does not delete. Namespace reset (hsfNSDELETE) wipes only up to 512 HookState entries per transaction — large state requires repeated transactions. Specified Namespace/Parameters/HookOn become the HookDefinition defaults, but HookGrants do NOT become defaults and are replaced wholesale when supplied.

capabilities.name: HookOn bitmap (active-low transaction-type trigger mask)
capabilities.summary: HookOn is a 256-bit field where each bit corresponds to a transaction-type code and decides whether the hook fires on that type. It uses active-LOW (inverted) semantics: a cleared bit means 'fire on this type'. Practically this means a hook configured to run on everything has most bits set the way you would not naively expect, and you flip specific bits to opt OUT of types. The sibling HookCanEmit field (added later) uses the same active-low scheme to whitelist which transaction types the hook is permitted to emit; if absent the hook may emit anything including SetHook.
key_fields: active-low bit per transaction type code
capabilities.gotchas: The inversion trips up nearly every newcomer — you do NOT set the bit for the type you want; you clear it. Toolkits expose helpers (e.g. invertHookOn / hooksdk constants) precisely to avoid hand-computing the mask. Getting HookOn wrong silently means the hook never runs on the transactions you cared about (no error — it just isn't triggered), so always verify against an explorer execution record.

capabilities.name: Hook API conventions & primitives (hook_account / otxn_* / return codes)
capabilities.summary: The Hook API is a fixed set of host functions the WASM module imports. Context accessors include hook_account (the account the hook is installed on), hook_hash, hook_pos (chain position), and hook_param/hook_param_set. The otxn_* family reads the originating transaction: otxn_field, otxn_id, otxn_type, otxn_burden, otxn_generation, otxn_slot, and otxn_param. Buffered functions write into a caller-supplied buffer and return a positive byte count on success or a negative error code (e.g. OUT_OF_BOUNDS, TOO_BIG, DOESNT_EXIST, GUARD_VIOLATION), so every call is checked by sign.
capabilities.gotchas: Return-value convention is sign-based, not exception-based — ignoring a negative return is the most common bug class. Slots are a limited resource (object handles); you must manage/free them. otxn_param reads parameters attached to the ORIGINATING transaction, which is distinct from hook_param (parameters set on the hook install) — confusing the two is a frequent error.

capabilities.name: Hook State (key-value store, namespaces, foreign reads)
capabilities.summary: Each account has a persistent key-value store accessed via state (read), state_set (write), and the cross-account state_foreign / state_foreign_set. Keys are always 32 bytes (a 256-bit integer) and values are variable length up to a validator-voted maximum — currently 256 bytes on mainnet (state_foreign_set was historically capped at 128 bytes on testnet). Namespaces (a 32-byte code) partition state so two hooks on the same account never collide; any hook may READ any other hook's state but only the owning hook may WRITE its own.
capabilities.gotchas: 256 bytes per value is tiny — you cannot store rich objects; you pack/encode (ABI-style) and often shard across multiple 32-byte keys, which then forces guarded loops. State writes cost reserve and fees, and the per-value max is governance-mutable (don't hardcode 256 as eternal). Foreign state is read-only across accounts — there is no cross-account write primitive.

best_for.purpose: Per-account counters, allowances, cooldowns, or rate limits enforced on-ledger
Tracking accumulated fees/royalties or running balances inside a hook
Storing a compact allowlist/flag set keyed by account

sources.title: Hook State | Xahau Network (ledger object)

sources.title: state_foreign_set (XRPL Hooks reference)
sources.claim: Any hook may read but not write another hook's state; state_foreign_set lets a hook write its own foreign-namespaced state, historically capped at 128 bytes on the public testnet pending validator voting.

capabilities.name: Loop guards — _g() / GUARD macro (bounded-execution requirement)
capabilities.summary: Hooks are deliberately non-Turing-complete: every loop must declare an iteration ceiling so the ledger can compute worst-case execution cost before running. The guard is _g(uint32_t id, uint32_t maxiter), wrapped by #define GUARD(maxiter) _g(__LINE__, (maxiter)+1) (the +1 covers the extra hit before the loop condition check). The first branch instruction after a loop MUST be a guard call, guards must use numeric literals (no runtime values), and nested-loop guards multiply (outer 3 × inner 5 → inner GUARD(15)). Exceeding the promise rolls the hook back with GUARD_VIOLATION.
capabilities.gotchas: An unguarded loop is rejected at compile/validation time by hook-cleaner — it will not even install. maxiter is a literal promise, NOT a runtime bound: you cannot guard with a variable, so data-driven iteration counts must be capped to a constant worst case (which inflates the fee). Forgetting that nested guards multiply is the classic source of silent under-budgeting and a runtime GUARD_VIOLATION.

best_for.purpose: Safely iterating a fixed-size packed state array inside a hook
Bounding any parsing/aggregation loop so the hook fee is deterministic

sources.title: Loops and Guarding (XRPL Hooks)
sources.claim: Signature is int32_t _g(uint32_t id, uint32_t maxiter); GUARD(maxiter) is defined as _g(__LINE__, (maxiter)+1); a _g call must be the first branch after a loop, maxiter must be a numeric literal, nested loops multiply, and violation triggers GUARD_VIOLATION rollback.

sources.title: Hooks overview — guards bound execution (Xahau Docs)
sources.claim: Xahau Hooks use guards so maximum execution time is well-bounded and known ahead of time, which is what makes the deterministic fee model possible.

capabilities.name: Emitted transactions — emit() / etxn_reserve / burden & generation
capabilities.summary: Hooks can autonomously originate NEW transactions via emit(), entered into consensus for the next ledger. A hook must first call etxn_reserve(n) to declare how many it will emit, then build the transaction (the PREPARE macro fills boilerplate) including an EmitDetails block instead of a signature; emitted txns have Sequence 0 and target the next ledger. Anti-fork-bomb controls: each emitted txn carries a generation (sfEmitGeneration, the chain depth, capped at 10) and a burden multiplier that raises cost exponentially for cascading emissions; FirstLedgerSequence must be the next ledger and LastLedgerSequence is capped ~5 ledgers ahead.
capabilities.gotchas: You must etxn_reserve BEFORE emitting and reserve the exact count — over/under reservation fails. Emitted transactions are NOT applied in the same ledger (they queue for the next), so a hook cannot read back the effect of its own emission in the same execution. The generation cap (10) and exponential burden mean deep emission chains become prohibitively expensive by design — emission is for one or two follow-up actions, not orchestration loops.

best_for.purpose: Auto-forwarding/splitting a payment (fee, royalty, tithe) when funds arrive
Reacting to an in-game event by minting/transferring a follow-up asset
Emitting an NFT transfer or offer acceptance as a side effect

capabilities.name: Hook chaining (up to 10 hooks per account)
capabilities.summary: An account can install a chain of up to 10 hooks at positions 0–9, executed in order; the chain succeeds only if every installed hook reaches accept(). Blank positions are skipped and treated as successful, so chains can be sparse. At runtime a hook can introspect and steer the chain: hook_pos() (own position), hook_skip() (disable/re-enable downstream hooks), hook_param_set() (pass parameters to later hooks), and hook_again() to request a second WEAK execution after the transaction applies. This enforces the 'each hook does one thing well' composition model.
capabilities.gotchas: Any single hook calling rollback() (or erroring) fails the WHOLE chain and the transaction — composition is AND, not OR. Both the sending and receiving account chains must succeed for a transaction between them to proceed. hook_again() schedules an extra weak pass that CANNOT rollback, so post-application logic there cannot undo the transaction.

best_for.purpose: Layering independent rules (allowlist + fee + rate-limit) as separate audited hooks
Composing economy guardrails without one monolithic hook
Reusing a shared fee hook alongside an account-specific hook

capabilities.name: Transactional stakeholders — strong vs weak execution
capabilities.summary: A Transactional Stakeholder (TSH) is any account affected by a transaction, and the model gives each the right to run hooks. STRONG TSHes (e.g. a Payment destination, a CheckCreate destination) have hooks executed BEFORE the transaction applies and can rollback() to block it; the originating transaction pays their fees. WEAK TSHes (e.g. rippled-through accounts, crossed-offer counterparties, a TrustSet issuer) execute AFTER application and cannot block — they must opt in via the asfTshCollect flag and pay through the collect-call mechanism. The reserved param tells the hook which context it is in (0 strong, 1 weak, 2 weak-after-strong).
key_fields: strong: pre-apply, can rollback, originator pays
weak: post-apply, cannot rollback, asfTshCollect opt-in
capabilities.gotchas: Whether your account is a STRONG or WEAK stakeholder for a given transaction type is fixed by protocol, not by you — and only strong stakeholders can actually block. If you need to enforce a rule and your account is merely a weak TSH for that transaction type, you cannot reject it; design around the strong-TSH positions. Weak execution requires the asfTshCollect flag set in advance or the weak hooks simply will not run.

best_for.purpose: Deciding where to place a blocking hook so it is actually a strong TSH
Enforcing receive-side rules on an account that is the Payment destination
Reacting (non-blocking) to NFT offer crossings as a weak stakeholder

capabilities.name: C/WASM toolchain & hook-cleaner (build pipeline)
capabilities.summary: The blessed production path is C compiled to WebAssembly. Toolkits (hooks-toolkit / @xahau/hooks-cli) compile contracts in a contracts/ directory to.wasm in build/; hook-cleaner post-processes the WASM to strip unsupported imports and verify the loop-guard invariant before SetHook will accept it. The browser-based Hooks Builder IDE lets you develop/test/debug/deploy to testnet. Alternative front-ends exist — hooks-rs (Rust) and assemblyscript paths — but C remains the reference and best-documented toolchain.
capabilities.gotchas: hook-cleaner is not optional — it enforces the guard rule and strips imports, and bytecode it rejects cannot be installed. WASM size and the limited import surface (only the Hook API host functions) mean standard C libraries are largely unavailable; you write against the hook ABI, not libc. Rust/AssemblyScript front-ends are real but less mature than the C path — prefer C for anything shipping.

capabilities.name: Hook fees & resource limits (deterministic up-front pricing)
capabilities.summary: Because guards make a hook's worst-case instruction count statically computable, Xahau prices hook execution deterministically UP FRONT (the worst case, not the actual path taken). The originating transaction must carry a Fee large enough to cover every strong hook's computed worst case plus reserved emissions; under-fee transactions are rejected before execution. Resource ceilings are governance (validator-vote) tuned: HookInstructionCount and HookEmitCount appear in execution metadata, state values are bounded (~256 bytes), and emission generation is capped at 10. Strong-hook fees fall on the originator; weak hooks collect via asfTshCollect.
capabilities.gotchas: You pay for the WORST case the guards declare, not the path actually executed — over-conservative guard ceilings inflate every transaction's fee, so tune maxiter tightly. Limits (state size, instruction count) are governance-mutable: do not hardcode them as constants in client logic. A transaction that under-budgets the fee is rejected outright; verify computed fees against an explorer execution record (HookInstructionCount/HookEmitCount) rather than guessing.

research.notes: Depth synthesis (mid-2026). Hooks are live on Xahau mainnet (L1 XRPL-core fork, mainnet since Oct 2023; the Hooks amendment is active and the network's own Genesis/reward economics run on Hooks). A Hook is a small WebAssembly module attached to an account that runs BEFORE and/or AFTER a transaction touches that account — it can accept(), rollback() (block) the originating transaction, mutate persistent Hook State, and emit() brand-new transactions of its own. This pre-transaction veto is the single most important property for game economies: a Hook decides whether a move is even allowed, unlike an EVM/L2 contract which can only react after value has already moved. Constraints are deliberate, not accidental: Hooks are NOT Turing-complete; every loop/branch must be GUARD()-ed with a compile-time-known max iteration count; ~64 KiB linear memory; fees are pre-computed from the worst-case execution duration (no surprise gas blowups) and paid by the caller; no access to wall-clock time or a real RNG (both are non-deterministic and would break consensus). State is a per-account key→value store, keys fixed at 32 bytes, values capped at 256 bytes (validator-voted), organised into namespaces; a Hook can READ another account's state via state_foreign() but can only WRITE its own. Up to 4 Hooks chain per account (positions 0-3). HookGrants let a Hook authorize OTHER accounts to write into its state — the mechanism behind shared registries (allowlists, ladders, leaderboards). Real, deployable references exist: Xahau/TreasuryHook (rate-limited vesting + reward forwarding), the documented Firewall Hook (foreign-state blocklist), and the Carbon/Doubler/Peggy example Hooks (emission patterns). JSHooks (JavaScript Hooks via a modified QuickJS-in-WASM runtime) is in alpha on a dedicated JSHooks testnet as of mid-2026 — promising for studio velocity but NOT yet a mainnet production path; ship WASM (C / Rust via hooks-rs) for anything that holds real value today. Decision frame for game logic: Hooks (L1, preventative, deterministic, fixed-fee, no Turing-completeness) for economy invariants and value gating; XRPL EVM sidechain (L2, mainnet since 30 Jun 2025, full Solidity/Turing-complete, retroactive only, bridge round-trip) for complex stateful game worlds and EVM-tooling reuse; native XRPL/Xahau objects (Escrow, Checks, AMM, NFTokens) when a built-in primitive already does the job with zero custom code.

capabilities.name: Hook accept/rollback as a pre-transaction economy gate
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (Hooks amendment active; L1)
capabilities.summary: The foundational primitive every game-economy Hook is built on: a Hook installed on an account runs before and/or after each transaction and returns either accept() (let it through) or rollback() (block it, reverting all effects). Because the Hook executes inside consensus on Layer 1, it can VETO a move before any value changes hands — block a disallowed transfer, reject an underpriced trade, refuse a payment that would break an invariant. This is categorically different from an EVM/L2 contract, which can only react after the originating transaction has already settled. A Hook can sit on the source account, the destination account, or both, and each can independently rollback. This is the lever that makes on-chain economy rules ENFORCEABLE rather than merely observable.
capabilities.key_fields: Hook entry function hook(uint32_t reserved) returns via accept(msg,len,code) or rollback(msg,len,code); HookOn bitmask selects which transaction types trigger the Hook; rollback() reverts ALL ledger effects of the triggering transaction including emitted txns; the originating account still pays the Hook execution fee even on rollback (anti-spam); a Hook on the destination account can block INBOUND transfers (e.g. refuse soulbound items), a Hook on the source blocks OUTBOUND.
capabilities.gotchas: rollback() is the ONLY way to block — there is no 'silently drop'; a blocked transaction still consumes the sender's fee, so design error messages/codes to be meaningful. A Hook only fires on transaction types enabled in HookOn; forgetting to set the right bit means the rule silently never runs. Hooks on an account apply to ALL counterparties uniformly — per-counterparty logic must be implemented in code + state, not by the trigger mechanism. The pre/after distinction matters: 'weak' (after) executions cannot rollback the originating txn.

best_for.purpose: Block disallowed transfers (soulbound items, banned wallets) before value moves
Reject underpriced or rule-violating trades at the ledger layer
Gate inbound payments on identity/credential checks

capabilities.name: Auto-route marketplace fees / tax / burn on transfer via a Hook
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (uses accept + emit; L1)
capabilities.summary: The canonical game-economy Hook: when value flows through an account, the Hook computes a percentage and routes it elsewhere — a marketplace fee to the studio treasury, a sales tax to a sink, or a burn that removes supply. The Hook reads the originating Payment amount, computes the cut using XFL (the deterministic integer-encoded float type), and either emit()s a follow-on Payment to the treasury or, for a burn, emits a payment to a blackholed sink (true protocol burn of XAH happens via fees, so 'burn' for game tokens means routing to an unspendable account). The documented Auto-Savings Hook ('send 10% of outgoing payments to savings') is the same shape. This replaces off-chain fee accounting with an invariant the ledger itself enforces — players literally cannot transact around the fee.
capabilities.key_fields: Reads sfAmount of the triggering Payment via otxn_field; computes cut with float_* / XFL math (no native floats — XFL is integer-encoded for determinism); emit() of a new Payment to the treasury/sink; etxn_reserve(n) must be called to declare emission count before emit(); HookParameters carry the fee basis-points and destination account so the same bytecode is reused with different config; trust-line (IOU) amounts vs native XAH amounts are encoded differently and need branch handling.
capabilities.gotchas: You cannot deduct the fee from the SAME payment in flight — the Payment amount is fixed; you either rollback() and require the sender to include the fee, or accept() the original and emit() a SECOND payment pulling the fee from the account (which needs the account to hold the funds and have the Hook authorized). Emitted payments cost an additional fee and count against etxn_reserve. XFL rounding must be deterministic and tested — a fee math bug is a real-value bug. For IOU/issued game currencies, transfer fees may ALSO be governed by the native TransferRate on the issuer; don't double-charge. A 'burn' to a sink is not a protocol-level supply reduction unless the asset is XAH consumed as fee.

best_for.purpose: Take a guaranteed marketplace cut to the studio treasury on every secondary sale
Apply an on-chain sink/tax to cool an inflationary in-game currency
Enforce a protocol-level fee that players cannot route around

capabilities.name: Hook-emitted reward distribution (autonomous payouts)
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (emit + cbak; L1)
capabilities.summary: A Hook can autonomously create transactions ('emitted transactions') on the account's behalf — the mechanism for trigger-driven reward distribution: a quest-completion Invoke triggers the Hook, which emit()s payouts to the winners; a treasury Hook forwards a claimed reward to a beneficiary. Xahau/TreasuryHook does exactly this in production: it forwards the monthly 4% claim reward to a configured destination account. Emitted transactions enter consensus for the NEXT ledger, carry a deterministic nonce so identical payouts get distinct hashes, and can register a cbak() callback that fires when the emission lands (or expires) — letting the Hook confirm a payout succeeded and update state accordingly. This turns the ledger into a self-executing payout engine with no off-chain cron job holding keys.
capabilities.key_fields: emit() submits the prepared txn; etxn_reserve(N) declares up to N emissions (must precede emit); etxn_nonce() supplies the deterministic nonce so duplicate payouts hash differently; cbak(uint32_t) callback fires on emission outcome (parameter=1 means the emitted txn expired); etxn_generation is capped at 10 to prevent emit-chains becoming fork bombs; etxn_burden grows the fee exponentially down an emission chain; EmitDetails (generation, burden, parent txn id, nonce, callback account) is auto-populated and must be present.
capabilities.gotchas: Emissions are NOT instant — they settle in a later ledger, so a reward isn't final at the moment the Hook runs; design for the cbak (or expiry) rather than assuming success. The 10-generation cap means deep recursive payout fan-outs will be cut off. Each emission costs fee and reserve; a Hook that tries to pay 500 winners in one go will exhaust etxn_reserve — batch or paginate across triggers. Emitted txns must have Sequence=0 and no signature; eight strict emission rules are validated and any violation aborts the emit. The emitting account must actually HOLD the funds being paid out.

best_for.purpose: Pay quest/tournament winners automatically on a trigger transaction
Forward claimed rewards from a treasury to beneficiaries with on-ledger receipts
Distribute revenue-share to many recipients (batched across triggers)

capabilities.name: On-chain invariant / anti-cheat checks at the ledger layer
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (accept/rollback + state; L1)
capabilities.summary: Because a Hook runs inside consensus and can rollback(), it can enforce economy invariants that a client or off-chain server could be tricked into violating — the on-ledger anti-cheat layer. Patterns: refuse a sell if the seller doesn't actually own the item (verify via state or ledger objects), reject a craft that would mint more than a supply cap (check a counter in Hook State), block a transfer that would push a balance negative or above a per-account holding limit, refuse a move that doesn't match a committed game-state hash. The check is deterministic and runs identically on every validator, so there is no trusted server to compromise. This does NOT validate off-chain gameplay (the Hook can't see your render loop) — it validates the ON-CHAIN consequences, which is exactly where value-affecting cheats land.
capabilities.key_fields: rollback() on invariant violation; supply/holding counters in Hook State (32-byte key, ≤256-byte value) updated atomically within the same execution; state_foreign() to read another account's authoritative state (e.g. an issuer's supply registry) read-only; otxn_field to inspect the triggering txn's amount/destination/memos; sfHookEmitCount and ledger-object reads to confirm true ownership; GUARD()-bounded loops if iterating a small fixed set of checks.
capabilities.gotchas: A Hook only sees what is ON the ledger or in its state — it cannot validate physics, hidden information, or anything the client computed off-chain; treat it as a value-integrity gate, not a full game referee. State writes are limited to your OWN account; cross-account invariants need either state_foreign reads or HookGrants. 256-byte value cap means large game states must be hashed/sharded, not stored whole. Every invariant loop must be GUARD()-ed with a compile-time max — you cannot iterate an unbounded player list inside one execution. If two Hooks in a chain both check, ordering (positions 0-3) matters.

best_for.purpose: Enforce a hard mint/supply cap that no client bug can exceed
Reject sells/transfers of items the actor doesn't truly own on-ledger
Verify a move against a committed on-chain state commitment

capabilities.name: Hook-enforced escrow, vesting and rate-limited release
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (TreasuryHook is a deployed reference; L1)
capabilities.summary: Where native Escrow/Checks are too rigid (fixed amount, single release), a Hook implements programmable vesting and rate limiting: cap how much value can leave an account per ledger interval, drip a vesting schedule, or throttle an action to N-per-window. Xahau/TreasuryHook is the production reference — it voluntarily locks the treasury so at most a configured amount of XAH (parameter A, XFL) can leave per configured ledger interval (parameter L), enforced on Invoke transactions, with the account effectively blackholed so funds can ONLY exit through the rule. The same shape gives a game: founder/team token vesting, staking-reward drip, faucet anti-drain, and 'one claim per day' mechanics — all enforced by the ledger, not a backend.
capabilities.key_fields: Window accounting in Hook State: store last-release ledger index + cumulative-released-this-window; compare current ledger_seq against stored index to detect window rollover; parameters A=max amount (XFL), L=ledger interval, D=destination (TreasuryHook convention); rollback() when over the cap, accept()+emit() the allowed release; account blackholed (regular key disabled) so the Hook is the only spend path; ledger sequence (NOT wall-clock time) is the time source because clock time is non-deterministic.
capabilities.gotchas: Time = ledger sequence, not seconds; a 'daily' limit is really 'every N ledgers' and ledger close time drifts slightly. Blackholing the account is irreversible — if the Hook has a bug the funds are stuck behind it forever, so audit before locking. Native Escrow/PaymentChannel may be simpler and cheaper if you only need a single time-locked release — reach for a Hook only when you need ongoing rate limiting or conditional logic native objects can't express. Window counters live in 256-byte state values; keep the schema tight. Reward forwarding (TreasuryHook) needs a SECOND companion Hook (genesis-mint) — multi-Hook coordination adds deployment complexity.

Rate-limit treasury outflow / prevent a faucet from being drained
Enforce 'one claim per window' game mechanics without a backend

capabilities.name: Shared allowlist / blocklist registries via foreign state + HookGrants
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (state_foreign + HookGrants; L1)
capabilities.summary: A Hook can READ another account's Hook State (state_foreign), so one account can publish a list and MANY accounts' Hooks can enforce it without each maintaining a copy — the documented Firewall Hook does this, pulling an updated blocklist from a Hook on a separate registry account to reject scam/suspicious transactions automatically. Inverted, it's an allowlist: only let transfers proceed to/from accounts present in a curated registry (whitelisted players, KYC-passed wallets, partner marketplaces). HookGrants is the complement: a registry Hook can authorize specific OTHER accounts to WRITE into its state, enabling a moderated, multi-writer registry (e.g. several studio admin accounts can add/remove entries) while normal players cannot.
capabilities.key_fields: state_foreign(key, namespace, foreign_account) reads the registry account's state read-only; HookGrants array authorizes named accounts to write into THIS Hook's state (set via SetHook Update); namespace isolates the registry's storage; 32-byte keys map naturally to account-id-derived keys for O(1) membership tests; rollback() when an actor is absent from an allowlist or present on a blocklist; the registry is one account, enforcing Hooks live on many accounts.
capabilities.gotchas: Foreign state is READ-ONLY — enforcers can check the list but only the owner (or HookGrant-authorized accounts) can change it; key compromise of the registry account is a single point of failure for every enforcer that trusts it. There is no native 'iterate all entries' — model membership as direct key lookups, not scans, because loops are GUARD-bounded. A 256-byte value holds limited data per entry; large lists are many keys, and namespace reset clears at most 512 entries per transaction. Allowlist enforcement only covers ON-CHAIN actions; it can't stop off-chain account sharing.

best_for.purpose: Block known scam/banned wallets from interacting with game accounts
Restrict marketplace/transfers to a curated allowlist of verified players
Maintain one shared registry many accounts enforce without duplicating it

capabilities.name: Time / rate limiting actions by ledger sequence
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (state + ledger_seq; L1)
capabilities.summary: Hooks have no wall-clock (it is non-deterministic), so 'time' for any cooldown, cadence, or rate limit is the ledger sequence number / last-closed-ledger info, which is part of consensus and identical on every validator. The pattern: store the ledger index of the last allowed action in Hook State, and on the next trigger compare the current ledger sequence — reject (rollback) if not enough ledgers have elapsed, otherwise accept and overwrite the stored index. This implements cooldowns (one action per ~N ledgers), token-bucket throttles, daily-claim caps, and auction/round timers entirely on-ledger. It is the timing backbone shared by the vesting and faucet patterns.
capabilities.key_fields: Current ledger sequence read from ledger/transaction context (ledger_last_time / ledger_seq family); last-action ledger index stored per actor in Hook State (key derived from actor account id); delta = current_seq - stored_seq compared against an interval parameter; token-bucket = stored (tokens, last-refill-ledger) tuple refilled proportional to elapsed ledgers; rollback() with a descriptive code when rate exceeded.
capabilities.gotchas: Ledger close interval is roughly a few seconds but NOT exactly constant — never assume a fixed seconds-per-ledger; express limits in ledgers and document the approximate wall-time. Per-actor counters mean one state entry per active actor — for a huge player base this grows state; consider expiring stale entries. You cannot use the network clock or any external time oracle. Reading the wrong context field (closing vs last-closed ledger) introduces off-by-one timing bugs that are subtle to catch. Because it's deterministic, every validator agrees — but so does every griefer, who can predict exactly when a window opens.

best_for.purpose: Enforce action cooldowns / one-per-window claims on-ledger
Throttle spammy or extractive transactions with a token bucket
Drive on-ledger round/auction timers

capabilities.name: On-chain randomness via deterministic nonce (and why true RNG is impossible)
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (etxn_nonce / ledger-hash seed; L1)
capabilities.summary: There is NO true randomness available to a Hook, by design: every validator must compute the identical result for consensus, so a real RNG would fork the network. What exists is a DETERMINISTIC pseudo-random nonce — etxn_nonce() — seeded by the last-closed ledger hash plus the Hook's account, advanced each call up to a max-call limit. It exists primarily to give emitted transactions distinct hashes, but it's the same value people reach for when they want 'randomness' for loot rolls or matchmaking. The critical caveat for game designers: the seed (last ledger hash) is PUBLIC and can be observed before a transaction is included, and validators have some influence over ledger contents — so anything financially meaningful (rare-drop gacha, jackpots) is manipulable/predictable and must NOT rely on this for fairness. For high-stakes randomness, use a commit-reveal scheme or an external verifiable randomness oracle, not the on-chain nonce alone.
capabilities.key_fields: etxn_nonce() returns a deterministic 32-byte nonce; PRNG seed = last-closed-ledger hash + Hook account; advanced per call, capped at a max number of calls per execution; ledger_last_hash exposed as deterministic seed material; for fairness use commit-reveal (commit a hashed secret one ledger, reveal next) or an off-chain VRF/oracle providing externally verifiable entropy.
capabilities.gotchas: DO NOT use the deterministic nonce for anything an adversary profits from predicting — the seed is observable and partially influenceable; treat it as 'unique-ish', not 'fair'. The nonce has a per-execution call cap; you cannot generate unlimited draws. Commit-reveal adds latency (at least one ledger between commit and reveal) and a griefing surface (a player can refuse to reveal an unfavorable outcome — design forfeiture). True VRF/oracle randomness means an external dependency and trust assumptions, which partly defeats the point of L1 enforcement. Many naive 'on-chain RNG' designs from other chains are insecure for the same reason and should not be copied.

best_for.purpose: Generate unique nonces / hashes for emitted transactions
Low-stakes cosmetic variation where predictability doesn't matter
High-stakes fair loot/jackpot rolls (NOT suitable — use commit-reveal/VRF)

capabilities.name: What Hooks CANNOT do — the deliberate non-Turing-complete envelope
capabilities.network_status: live on Xahau mainnet (design constraints of the Hooks amendment; L1)
capabilities.summary: Hooks are intentionally constrained, and knowing the walls prevents designing a game system that can't ship. Hard limits as of mid-2026: NOT Turing-complete (no unbounded computation); every loop/branch must be GUARD()-ed with a compile-time-known max iteration count (no while-true); ~64 KiB linear memory; no wall-clock, no real RNG, no network/IO, no calls except the Hook API; state values capped at 256 bytes, keys 32 bytes; at most 4 Hooks chain per account; emitted-transaction chains capped at 10 generations; fees are pre-computed from the worst-case duration. The flip side is what you GAIN: predictable bounded fees (no gas blowups or out-of-gas reverts mid-state), guaranteed termination (no halting-problem DoS), deterministic replay, and tiny attack surface. Anything needing big in-contract state, arbitrary loops, complex math libraries, or composable DeFi-style call graphs is OUT of scope — that's the EVM sidechain's job.
capabilities.key_fields: GUARD(maxiter) required before every back-edge; ~64 KiB WASM linear memory; non-Turing-complete by design; HookState value ≤256 bytes, key =32 bytes; ≤4 Hooks per account (positions 0-3); etxn_generation ≤10; fee proportional to MAX computed execution duration, paid by caller even on rollback; only the Hook API is callable (no syscalls, no floats — use XFL); no contract-to-contract synchronous calls (composition is via emitted txns + foreign-state reads, asynchronously).
capabilities.gotchas: The single biggest trap is assuming EVM mental models port over: there are no synchronous cross-contract calls, no big mappings, no arbitrary loops, no msg.sender-style reentrancy (composition is async via emit). 256-byte state forces hashing/sharding for anything large. GUARD makes some algorithms (sorting an arbitrary list, unbounded search) simply unimplementable in one execution. Porting a Solidity game contract 1:1 will fail — redesign around accept/rollback + state + emit. JSHooks may relax the authoring ergonomics but NOT the consensus-level limits (still bounded, deterministic).

best_for.purpose: Decide upfront whether a game rule fits the Hooks envelope before building
Avoid gas-style failure modes by relying on pre-computed bounded fees
Recognise when to push complex logic to the EVM sidechain instead

capabilities.name: Hooks vs EVM sidechain vs native objects — choosing the game-logic layer
capabilities.network_status: Hooks live on Xahau L1; XRPL EVM sidechain mainnet since 30 Jun 2025; native objects live on both XRPL & Xahau
capabilities.summary: Three places to put game logic, and the choice is load-bearing. (1) Hooks (Xahau L1): preventative — can veto a transaction before value moves; deterministic; bounded fixed fees; non-Turing-complete; tightly integrated with native ledger objects; ideal for economy invariants, fee routing, gating, vesting, anti-cheat. (2) XRPL EVM sidechain (L2, mainnet since 30 Jun 2025): full Solidity/Turing-complete with the whole EVM tool ecosystem, but RETROACTIVE only (it reacts after a txn settles) and requires bridging value onto the sidechain and back; ideal for complex stateful game worlds, arbitrary loops/math, and reusing EVM dev talent. (3) Native objects (Escrow, Checks, PaymentChannels, AMM, NFTokens, Credentials/DepositPreauth): zero custom code, audited, cheapest — use when a built-in primitive already does the job. Rule of thumb: native first if a primitive fits; Hooks when you need to ENFORCE a rule at the moment of transaction; EVM when the logic is genuinely complex/stateful and a retroactive L2 is acceptable.
capabilities.key_fields: Hooks = L1, pre-transaction veto, deterministic, GUARD-bounded, fixed fee, WASM (or JSHooks alpha); EVM sidechain = L2, post-settlement, Turing-complete Solidity, bridge round-trip, gas-metered, mainnet 2025-06-30; native objects = no code, protocol-audited, cheapest; decision axes = preventative-vs-retroactive, deterministic-fixed-fee-vs-gas, integration-with-XAH-vs-bridged, complexity ceiling, dev-skill availability (XRPL-native vs Solidity).
capabilities.gotchas: EVM contracts CANNOT block the originating ledger transaction — if you need to stop a bad move before it lands, that's Hooks/native only. Bridging to the EVM sidechain adds latency, a trust/bridge-risk surface, and round-trip cost — don't move value across a bridge for logic a Hook could enforce in place. Don't write a custom Hook when native Escrow/Credentials already cover the case (wasted audit risk). Don't try to force complex Turing-complete game simulation into Hooks — it won't fit the envelope. The two chains are SEPARATE networks; assets/state don't share a ledger, so a hybrid game must design the bridge boundary explicitly.

best_for.purpose: Pick the right layer for an economy rule (preventative L1 vs retroactive L2 vs native)
Decide payment-flow enforcement location
Plan a hybrid architecture spanning Xahau Hooks and the EVM sidechain

capabilities.name: JSHooks — JavaScript Hooks authoring (alpha, mid-2026)
capabilities.network_status: alpha on dedicated JSHooks testnet (modified QuickJS-in-WASM); NOT yet mainnet as of mid-2026
capabilities.summary: JSHooks lets Hooks be written in plain JavaScript (and TypeScript, compiled to JS) instead of C/Rust-to-WASM, by running a modified QuickJS engine compiled to WASM as the execution runtime. For a small studio this is a big velocity unlock — gameplay/economy logic in a familiar language, faster iteration, lower the bar for the crew. As of mid-2026 it is ALPHA: there is a dedicated JSHooks testnet with a live explorer, the jshooks-alpha toolkit ('expect dragons'), and the QuickJS runtime build, but it is NOT enabled on Xahau mainnet. The same consensus-level constraints still apply (deterministic, bounded, no real RNG/time) — JSHooks changes the authoring language, not the execution envelope. For anything holding real value today, ship compiled WASM (C, or Rust via hooks-rs); treat JSHooks as a watch-this-space prototyping path.
capabilities.key_fields: Modified QuickJS runtime compiled to WASM (qjsc.wasm) executes the JS; toolkit compiles .js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts to SetHook-ready hook code (TS → JS first); dedicated JSHooks testnet + XRPLWin JSHooks explorer + JSHook Builder (XWCode); same Hook API surface (accept/rollback/state/emit) exposed to JS; consensus constraints unchanged (deterministic, GUARD-equivalent bounding, no clock/RNG).
capabilities.gotchas: NOT mainnet — do not architect a shipping game's value layer on JSHooks until the amendment activates on Xahau mainnet; it can change. 'Expect dragons' is the maintainers' own framing — alpha bugs, breaking changes, incomplete API parity. The QuickJS runtime adds overhead vs hand-written WASM; fee/performance characteristics may differ from compiled hooks. JS's dynamic nature does not exempt you from determinism — non-deterministic JS (Date.now, Math.random) is unavailable/forbidden. Production today = WASM (C / Rust hooks-rs); use JSHooks for prototyping and to track the roadmap.

best_for.purpose: Prototype economy/game Hook logic quickly in JS/TS on testnet
Lower the authoring bar for a small crew (familiar language)
Ship a mainnet value-bearing Hook (NOT yet — use WASM)
